title: Respiratory System

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the structure and function of the upper and lower respiratory tract.
- Explain the process of gas exchange in the lungs and its purpose.
- Recognize common respiratory conditions and the basic terms used to describe them.
- Apply respiratory knowledge to safe office communication, documentation, and escalation.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the airway like a hallway into a building. The upper part is the entrance near your nose and throat, and the lower part is the long tunnels that go deep into your chest where the lungs are.

### Question 2

It is like a slide at the park: the air gets on at your nose, slides past your throat and voice box, and then whooshes down the windpipe into your lungs.

### Question 3

Your nose works like a furnace and a strainer combined: it warms the air and catches dust and germs before they get into your lungs.

### Question 4

Picture the airways as a sticky conveyor belt: mucus catches the dust, and tiny hairs sweep the belt upward to carry the dirt out of your body.

### Question 5

Your throat is like a two-way street where two trains pass through: air goes down one tunnel (toward the lungs) and food goes down the other (toward the stomach).

### Question 6

The larynx is like a guitar inside your neck: when air blows across the strings (vocal cords), they vibrate and make your voice.

### Question 7

The epiglottis is like a trapdoor that closes over the windpipe when you swallow, so your food goes to your stomach instead of into your lungs.

### Question 8

The windpipe is the sturdy tube you can sometimes feel in the front of your neck; it is the main hallway that air uses to reach your lungs.

### Question 9

Imagine the windpipe as a stack of horseshoe-shaped rings. The gap in each horseshoe faces the food tube, so the food tube can stretch when you swallow a big bite.

### Question 10

The carina is like the fork in a road where one big tunnel splits into two smaller tunnels, one going to each lung.

### Question 11

It is like a slide: the right tunnel is straighter and steeper, so a marble (or a bit of food) is more likely to roll down the right side.

### Question 12

Picture a tree turned upside down: the trunk (trachea) splits into big branches (bronchi), then twigs (bronchioles), and finally leaves (alveoli).

### Question 13

Your lungs live inside your chest, like two balloons tucked safely inside a cage of ribs, above the big muscle called the diaphragm.

### Question 14

The left lung is a little smaller and has a spot carved out so your heart can fit next to it, like making room on a shelf for a big jar.

### Question 15

The pleural fluid is like oil on a door hinge: it lets the lungs glide back and forth inside the chest without rubbing or sticking.

### Question 16

The diaphragm is like a big trampoline under your lungs. When it flattens down, your lungs get more room to fill with air.

### Question 17

These muscles are like little springs between your ribs that help your ribcage open up and close down as you breathe.

### Question 18

Breathing in is like pulling the handle of a bicycle pump: the diaphragm pulls down, making the space bigger, and air rushes in to fill it.

### Question 19

Breathing out is like letting go of a stretched rubber band: you do not push; the lungs snap back on their own and air flows out.

### Question 20

The alveoli are like millions of tiny bubbles at the very end of the airway, where the air and your blood get close enough to swap gases.

### Question 21

Think of a balloon made of super-thin skin covered in tiny red threads (blood vessels). Gases can slip right through the thin skin between the air and the blood.

### Question 22

Surfactant is like dish soap for your lungs: it keeps the tiny air bubbles from sticking shut, so they can pop open again and again with every breath.

### Question 23

Your lungs are like a trading post: oxygen comes in from the air and is traded for carbon dioxide, which is the body's waste gas that you breathe out.

### Question 24

Oxygen is like a crowd moving from a packed room (the air) into an emptier room (the blood), always flowing to where there is less of it.

### Question 25

Carbon dioxide is like trash being taken out: the blood carries it to the lungs, where it steps out into the air so you can blow it away.

### Question 26

External respiration is the swap that happens where the air meets the blood inside the lungs; internal respiration is the swap where the blood meets the body's cells.

### Question 27

It is like opening a door between a crowded room and an empty one; people naturally drift to the emptier side without anyone pushing them.

### Question 28

Hemoglobin is like a school bus inside each red blood cell: it gives oxygen a seat and drives it around the body to every part that needs it.

### Question 29

When carbon dioxide dissolves in the blood, most of it gets packed into a special 'backpack' called bicarbonate so the blood can carry lots of it back to the lungs.

### Question 30

Imagine drying a giant towel: the more thin, wet surface you spread out, the faster it dries. The lungs spread out an enormous thin, moist surface so gases can pass quickly.

### Question 31

If the trading post in your lungs gets blocked, less oxygen gets delivered and your body runs low on fuel, like a car with a clogged air filter.

### Question 32

If you count how many times someone breathes in half a minute, you just double that number to find out how many times they breathe in a whole minute.

### Question 33

Deep in your brain there is a tiny automatic drummer that keeps the beat of your breathing, working all day and all night without you having to think about it.

### Question 34

Your body has tiny carbon dioxide detectors that act like a smoke alarm; when waste gas builds up, they ring and tell your brain to breathe faster.

### Question 35

A cough is like a sudden blast of air that acts as a broom, sweeping dust and gunk out of your breathing tubes.

### Question 36

It is like an escalator that only goes up: the sticky mucus rides the moving hairs upward and out of your lungs, carrying germs and dust with it.

### Question 37

When you run, your muscles burn more fuel and make more waste, so your body turns up the breathing dial to bring in more oxygen and carry away more waste gas.

### Question 38

Carbon dioxide acts a little like acid bubbles in your blood; breathing them out keeps the blood from getting too acidic, like venting steam from a pot.

### Question 39

'A-' means 'without,' and 'pnea' means breathing, so apnea means a pause where no breathing is happening at all.

### Question 40

Asthma is like your breathing tubes getting squeezed and puffy, like a straw being pinched, so the air has a harder time squeezing through and makes a whistling sound.

### Question 41

Certain things in the air, like smoke or pollen, can act like a switch that makes asthma airways squeeze shut.

### Question 42

COPD is a big name for lungs that have slowly lost their stretchiness and get clogged, making it harder and harder to push air out over time.

### Question 43

Emphysema is like popping too many of the tiny bubbles in a sponge; with fewer bubbles left, there is less surface for the air and blood to meet.

### Question 44

Pneumonia is like your lung's tiny air bubbles filling up with liquid instead of air, so the air cannot get in and out the way it should.

### Question 45

Acute bronchitis is like your bronchial tubes getting irritated and swollen for a short time, usually by a virus, making you cough for a while.

### Question 46

A cold is usually a runny-nose nuisance, while the flu is like a bigger storm that makes your whole body ache, gives you a fever, and knocks you flat.

### Question 47

A cold is like a tiny, short-lived bug that visits your nose and throat, makes them runny and sore, and then usually leaves on its own.

### Question 48

TB is a germ that travels through the air when a sick person coughs, and it can make someone cough for a very long time if it is not treated.

### Question 49

Normally the lung is like a balloon held open inside the chest; a pneumothorax is air leaking into the space outside the balloon and squashing it flat.

### Question 50

A pleural effusion is like water pooling between a balloon and the box around it, squeezing the balloon and making it harder to inflate.

### Question 51

Sleep apnea is like a nighttime roller coaster where a person's breathing stops and starts again over and over, so they never get truly restful sleep.

### Question 52

Allergic rhinitis is like your nose overreacting to harmless dust or pollen by sneezing and running, as if it is trying to wash the irritants away.

### Question 53

When your voice box (larynx) gets swollen, your vocal cords cannot vibrate properly, so your voice comes out rough or disappears.

### Question 54

Epiglottitis is when the little trapdoor that protects your windpipe swells up so much it could block your breathing, which is why it is an emergency.

### Question 55

Breathing in smoke over many years is like constantly blowing soot into a machine; it wears out the lungs and can lead to serious disease.

### Question 56

Stridor sounds like a high whistle when breathing in, a warning that the top part of the breathing tube is getting too narrow.

### Question 57

Crackles sound like the snap-crackle-pop of cereal or a fire; they can mean there is extra fluid in the tiny air sacs.

### Question 58

When the blood does not carry enough oxygen, the skin can turn a little blue, like a cold pair of lips, which is the body's way of signaling trouble.

### Question 59

Sputum is the gunk you cough up from your lungs; its color and thickness can give clues about what is going on inside.

### Question 60

Hypoxemia is low oxygen in the delivery truck (the blood), while hypoxia is low oxygen arriving at the stores (the tissues) that need it.

### Question 61

A pulse oximeter is a little clip that shines a light through your finger to see how full of oxygen your blood is, like checking how full a fuel gauge is.

### Question 62

Spirometry is like timing and measuring how much air you can blow out of your lungs, the way you might measure how much water a straw can move.

### Question 63

A peak flow meter is like a speedometer for your breath: it shows how fast you can blow, which helps track whether asthma is getting better or worse.

### Question 64

An incentive spirometer is like a breathing exercise game: you try to raise a little ball by taking a big, slow breath, which keeps your lungs open and healthy.

### Question 65

If the little light on the finger clip is blocked by cold, nail polish, or wiggling, it cannot read the blood properly, like trying to read through a foggy window.

### Question 66

If the fuel gauge on a car drops into the red, you tell the mechanic right away; the assistant does the same by telling the clinician about a low oxygen reading.

### Question 67

In medical words, 'pneum/o' and 'pulmon/o' are two different keys that open the same door: they both mean lung.

### Question 68

If you see 'rhin/o,' think of a rhino's big nose; it means nose.

### Question 69

The assistant writes down exactly what the patient says and observes, like a careful note-taker, but leaves the 'what does this mean' part to the doctor or nurse.

### Question 70

If someone says they suddenly cannot breathe well, that is like a fire alarm; the assistant's job is to call for help right away, not to guess.

### Question 71

When someone is coughing, the assistant helps keep germs from traveling by offering a mask and cleaning hands, like putting a lid on a sneeze.

### Question 72

Blue lips and gasping for air are like a five-alarm fire; the assistant drops everything and gets the trained helpers right away.

### Question 73

The inhaler is like a tiny spray that squirts medicine into the breathing tubes to help them open up, but only the doctor decides how much and how often.

### Question 74

Think of 95 to 100 as the 'full tank' zone; a reading of 88 is below that, so the assistant shows it to the clinician right away.

### Question 75

A red-zone peak flow reading is like a speedometer in the danger zone; it means the patient should follow their emergency plan right away and get help.

### Question 76

The assistant talks like a friendly translator, turning big medical words into everyday words and checking that the patient really gets it.

### Question 77

When a person can only gasp out a few words at a time, it is a sign their breathing is getting worse, like an engine sputtering and about to stall.
